format: HYB-Exxxx registry (SPEC-LANGUAGE.md §9.6; append-only, never renumbered, never reused)

categories.E8: lint (warnings-only; can never fail the build)

codes.name: identifier-case
codes.title: Hybrid identifiers are snake_case
codes.summary: UpperCamelCase identifiers are rejected at binding time; foreign Go/Rust names are normalized when imported (SPEC M4).
fixits: rename the identifier to snake_case, e.g. `worker_id` instead of `WorkerID`
codes.example: WorkerID := 3   // reject: HYB-E0001 — write `worker_id`

codes.name: parse-error
codes.title: the program did not parse
codes.summary: Generic parse/lex error (the lexer's identifier-case violations keep HYB-E0001; everything else lands here). The diagnostic points at the failure site with the unexpected token named; recovery happens at the statement/declaration boundary.
fixits: read the pointed-to site — the unexpected token is named in the message
check the line above: unterminated braces, strings, or missing separators surface on the following line
codes.example: x := // reject: HYB-E0002 — expected expression, found end of line

codes.name: managed-payload-required
codes.title: managed blocks need a reason and a category
codes.summary: The escape hatch must be review-visible: a bare `managed { ... }` (or an empty reason/category) is a reject, not a lint — what the hatch bypasses and why must be IN the program (discussion #4, PLAN row 14; fail-closed like the boundary rule FC).
fixits: add the payload: managed("why this bypass is safe", "category") { ... }
pick the category from the closed set: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other
codes.example: managed { counts := map[string]int{} }   // reject: HYB-E0003 — write managed("shared map across tasks", "mutex") { ... }

codes.name: managed-unknown-category
codes.title: unknown managed category
codes.summary: The category is a CLOSED set so reviewers know which invariant a block bypasses without reading prose (discussion #4). Unknown categories are rejected; `other` exists for everything else and requires the reason to carry the specifics.
fixits: use one of the closed set: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other
codes.example: managed("r", "misc") { ... }   // reject: HYB-E0004 — `misc` is not a category; use `other` and put the specifics in the reason

codes.name: unresolved-name
codes.title: name is not available in this scope
codes.summary: The name is not declared, not imported, or not visible here. Some builtin names (e.g. `error`) require their package to be imported first.
fixits: import the package that declares it
check the spelling (foreign names are normalized to snake_case at binding time)
codes.example: fn f() error { return nil }  // reject: HYB-E1001 until `errors` is imported

codes.name: unbuildable-declaration
codes.title: the emitted Go cannot build this declaration
codes.summary: Go's front-end rejects five shapes that `hyb check` used to accept with 0 diagnostics, so the emitted module could never build. Issue #134 landed the first three: (1) an unused `:=` binding — `x := 5` with no read of `x` is `declared and not used`, and `_ := 5` / `_, _ := ...` declares no new variable at all (`no new variables on left side of :=`); (2) an unused import — the emitter carries every declared Go import into the header, and Go rejects `imported and not used`; (3) a repeated name on the left of one `:=` — `x, x := 1, 2` is `x repeated on left side of :=`. The #577 accept-side oracle wave added two more call/return shapes: (4) a call whose argument count disagrees with the callee — `add(1)` for `fn add(a int, b int) int` is `not enough arguments`, `add(1, 2, 3)` is `too many arguments`, and the same holds for a method (`x.bump()`) and a closure or `fn`-typed value whose declared parameter count is known; (5) a `return` that does not match the enclosing signature — a value list whose length differs from the declared results (except Go's naked `return` with all-named results, and a short return in a function whose last result is `error`, which the emitter zero-fills as E3's sugar), or a returned value whose type cannot be assigned to its result (`return "s"` from a `fn f() int`). Fail-closed: what the checker accepts must survive `go build`. Out of scope (same Go error family, separate issues): unused `var`/composite-`const` locals, select-receive names, unread `for ... in` bindings (handled at emission, issue #139), unused `rust/` imports (never emitted as Go imports), and return-type mismatches that need type-level rather than kind-level information (`int8` variable returned from an `int` function) — those stay fail-open so no buildable program is rejected.
fixits: read the binding — a mention anywhere in the function counts, including inside a closure, and `x++`, `x += 1`, `x[k] = v`, `x.f = v`, `&x` and `_ = x` all count (a bare `x = v` store does not); or drop the declaration
`_` is not a variable: `_ := 5` can never build — write `_ = 5` to discard the value, or bind a real name
remove the unused import (the emitted header carries it, and an unused import never builds)
give each name on the left of `:=` once: `x, y := 1, 2`
pass one argument per declared parameter — the receiver is not an argument, and a `fn`-typed field or closure states its own count
return exactly the declared results — name them if a naked `return` is intended, or end the signature with `error` to use the short-return sugar the emitter zero-fills
codes.example: x := 5   // reject: HYB-E1002 — `x` is never read; Go refuses the emitted `x := 5`

codes.name: redeclaration
codes.title: name is already declared in this block
codes.summary: Go keeps a single package block: top-level fns, consts, structs, enums, and types share one namespace, so a second declaration of the same name is `X redeclared in this block`. Struct fields must be unique within their struct, and a receiver type may declare each method name only once. Methods on DIFFERENT receiver types may share a name (they live in the receiver's method set, not package scope).
fixits: rename the second declaration
for a duplicate method, rename it or move it onto a second receiver type
for duplicate struct fields, rename one field
codes.example: fn main() {}  fn main() {}  // reject: HYB-E1003 — `main` redeclared in this block

codes.name: defer-non-call
codes.title: defer requires a call expression
codes.summary: `defer` of a non-call expression is a compile error.
fixits: defer the call itself: `defer f.close()?` instead of `defer f.close`
codes.example: defer f.close   // reject: HYB-E2001 — defer of a non-call

codes.name: multi-value-not-tuple
codes.title: a multi-value return is not a tuple
codes.summary: Hybrid has no tuples (T23). A function returning two values can only appear in a define (`a, b := f()`), a return, or an if-init — never as a single value.
fixits: bind both values: `lo, hi := minmax(3, 9)`
codes.example: p := minmax(3, 9)   // reject: HYB-E2002 — multi-value is not a tuple

codes.name: builtin-argument-invalid
codes.title: invalid argument to a builtin
codes.summary: A builtin call (`make`, `len`, `cap`, `delete`, `close`, `new`) with a compile-time-detectable bad arity or literal argument is rejected: Go refuses to compile the emitted call, so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #187). Only literal / arity misuse is in scope — variable operands stay a run-time concern, matching Go.
fixits: for `make`, pass a non-negative integer size (or omit size / use a variable); slices may also use the 3-argument form `make([]T, len, cap)`
for `len`/`cap`, pass a string, slice, map, array, or channel — not a number or bool literal
for `delete`, pass both the map and the key: `delete(m, k)`
for `close`, pass a channel value — not a literal
for `new`, pass a type name — not a value literal
codes.example: c := make(chan int, -1)   // reject: HYB-E2005 — make size must be a non-negative int

codes.name: equality-incomparable
codes.title: equality on a type Go cannot compare
codes.summary: Maps, slices, and function values have no `==`/`!=` in Go (`invalid operation: … can only be compared to nil`), and a struct is comparable only when every field is. Comparing such values passes `hyb check` but the emitted Go fails `go vet`/`go build`, violating the accepted-should-emit-buildable-Go contract (issue #201). Comparisons against `nil` are the nilable surface and are checked elsewhere (E4001).
fixits: for maps/slices: compare lengths or specific elements instead of whole-value equality
for function values: only `f == nil` is legal — compare behaviour by calling both
for structs: compare the comparable fields individually
codes.example: if m1 == m2 { … }  // reject: HYB-E2006 — maps cannot be compared

codes.name: invalid-receiver
codes.title: invalid method receiver type
codes.summary: A method receiver must be a defined (named) type or a single pointer to one — not a primitive (`int`), not an interface (`error`), not an anonymous type (slice/map/array/chan/fn), and never a double pointer (`**T`). Go rejects such declarations with `invalid receiver type`, so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #201).
fixits: declare the method on a struct (`struct box { … }` + `fn (b box) m()`)
or make it a plain fn (`fn m(x int)`)
for `**T`: use a single pointer receiver (`*T`)
codes.example: fn (c int) m() int { return c }  // reject: HYB-E2007 — primitive receiver

codes.name: receive-non-channel
codes.title: receive from a non-channel
codes.summary: `<-expr` where `expr` resolves to a concrete non-channel shape is rejected: a receive is only well-typed against a `chan T`, and the accepted-subset contract is that every accepted program emits buildable Go (issue #409 — the receive-side mirror of the send rule HYB-E3007, issue #77). `<-5`, `<-x` with `x` an int/map, and a receive from a non-channel call result used to pass with 0 diagnostics and then fail `go build` with `cannot receive from non-channel`. An UNRESOLVABLE source stays fail-closed under HYB-E3005 (O4.9), exactly as the send side treats an unknown target.
fixits: receive from a `chan T` binding (`ch := make(chan T, n)` or a `chan T` parameter)
bind the value first if it is a call result: `ch := make_call()` — then `<-ch`
a statement STARTING with `<-expr` is a receive — check the operand's type
codes.example: x := 5; <-x   // reject: HYB-E2008 — x is an int, not a channel

codes.name: non-iterable-range
codes.title: range over a non-iterable
codes.summary: `for x in e` where `e` resolves to a concrete non-iterable shape (int, bool, struct, pointer to a struct/slice/string, ...) is rejected: SPEC-LANGUAGE LX13 allows slices, arrays, strings (runes), maps (keys), and channels, and Go refuses `range` over anything else (a pointer TO AN ARRAY stays rangeable, mirroring Go's range rule), so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #411). The integer-range form `for i in 0..n` is a different statement kind and is not affected. An UNRESOLVABLE iterable stays fail-closed under HYB-E3005 (O4.9), exactly as the send (#77) and receive (#409) sides treat an unknown operand.
fixits: iterate a slice, array, string, map, or channel binding
for a number sequence use the integer-range form: `for i in 0..n`
for a function or method call result that resolves to an iterable, bind it to a local first so the checker can classify it
codes.example: x := 5; for v in x { }   // reject: HYB-E2009 — x is an int, not an iterable

codes.name: map-element-not-addressable
codes.title: store into part of a map element
codes.summary: A Go map element is not addressable: `m[k] = v` is legal, but a store into part of the element — `m[k].f = v`, `m[k].f += 1`, `m[k].f++`, `m[k][i] = v` on an array element, `m[k].arr[i] = v` — and an O8 loan whose store-back place is part of one (`n := &m[k].f`) emit Go that fails `go build` (`cannot assign to struct field m[k].f in map` / `neither addressable nor a map index expression`), violating the accepted-should-emit-buildable-Go contract. Only proven shapes reject: a pointer-typed or unresolved element stays legal.
fixits: take the whole slot as an O8 loan and store through it: `n := &m[k]; n.f = v`
copy the element out, modify it, and assign it back: `e := m[k]; e.f = v; m[k] = e`
codes.example: m["a"].bal = 9   // reject: HYB-E2010 — write `n := &m["a"]; n.bal = 9`

codes.name: not-sendable-spawn
codes.title: value is not sendable at a task spawn site
codes.summary: Only channels, atomics, immutable values, moved values, fresh literals of sendable parts, and `managed` values may cross a task spawn (Tier-0 rule O4: classes 1-6). A named mutable GC value (map, slice, struct, pointer-to-mutable) shared across tasks must go through a channel, a copy, an explicit `move`, or `managed`.
fixits: route updates through a channel instead of sharing the value
copy the data the task needs and send the copy
transfer ownership: `task worker(move counter)` — the binding (and every alias) must be unused afterward

wrap the shared state in `managed("why this bypass is safe", "category") { ... }` (unchecked: Go DRF-SC applies; audited by --report-managed; categories: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other)
codes.example: task worker(counter)   // reject: HYB-E3001 — `counter` is a mutable map

codes.name: not-sendable-send
codes.title: value is not sendable at a channel send
codes.summary: Same sendability classes as spawn sites (O4), enforced at every channel send. A fresh literal is only sendable when its reference-typed parts are sendable (O4.6 deep sendability).
fixits: send a copy or a fresh literal instead of a live shared value
send ownership with `move` if this task is done with the value (aliases freeze, O5)
share via channel discipline or wrap the site in `managed("why this bypass is safe", "category") { ... }` (audited by --report-managed; categories: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other)
codes.example: jobs <- job{input: v, data: shared_map}   // reject: HYB-E3002 — `shared_map` is a live mutable map

codes.name: use-after-move
codes.title: value used after ownership was moved away
codes.summary: After `move x` at a spawn/send/assignment/return — or after a consuming API call — the binding and every live alias are frozen: any use, read or write, is a use-after-move (O5.1/O5.2). Reads are included deliberately: the receiver may mutate concurrently, and Go's DRF-SC defines a concurrent unsynchronized read/write as a race.
fixits: compute what you need BEFORE the move and send it along
keep ownership here and send a copy
have the receiver report results back over a channel
codes.example: results <- move agg; agg["total"] = 1   // reject: HYB-E3003 — frozen alias

codes.name: move-on-gc-field
codes.title: move applies to whole bindings and own-handle fields, not GC fields
codes.summary: `move x.field` where the field is a slice/map/struct is rejected: the parent binding still aliases the storage, so the freeze cannot be sound (O5.4).
fixits: copy the field out and send the copy
move the whole value instead
codes.example: jobs <- move s.data   // reject: HYB-E3004 — move the whole `s` or copy `s.data`

codes.name: unproven-at-boundary
codes.title: value at a spawn/send boundary the checker could not prove safe (fail-closed)
codes.summary: The fail-closed boundary (O4.9, rule FC): a value whose type the checker could not resolve — an unresolvable name, an untyped unknown, an unsupported operation affecting ownership or cross-task sharing — used to pass silently; it no longer does. What the checker cannot prove is not called safe. Crossing the boundary requires making the type visible to the checker, or an explicit, auditable `managed` block (HYB-E8001, counted by --report-managed). This is what makes the Tier-0 guarantee a precise contract: everything the checker accepts is proven; everything else is named.
fixits: ascribe the type at the declaration (`var x map[string]int = ...`) so the checker can classify it
route the value through a channel of a known sendable element type instead of sharing it

if the share is genuinely guarded, wrap the site in `managed("why this bypass is safe", "category") { ... }` — the explicit, auditable hatch (counted by --report-managed; categories: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other)
codes.example: task handle(blob)          // reject: HYB-E3005 — blob's type did not resolve; the checker cannot prove it safe

codes.name: write-to-const
codes.title: cannot write to a `const` binding
codes.summary: `const` is a compile-time constant and the only DEEP immutability in MVP (SPEC-LANGUAGE T22): no rebind of the binding, no element/index write, no field store through it. A file-level `const` lowers to package-level state that every task body reaches ambiently, so an accepted write would be a data race carrying zero spawn-site evidence (issue #37). Reads stay legal — deep immutability bans the write, not the value.
fixits: make the value a `let`/`var` local and cross task boundaries with a proof (owned `move`, channel send, or `managed`)
keep the `const` and write to a local copy inside the task

if the state must be shared and updated, guard the access with `managed("why this is safe", "mutex"|"atomic"|"actor") { ... }` — the explicit, auditable hatch (categories: mutex, atomic, actor, finalizer, interop, other)
codes.example: const cells = [0]; cells[0] = cells[0] + 1   // reject: HYB-E3006 — `cells` is deeply immutable (T22)

codes.name: send-target-not-channel
codes.title: the target of a send must be a channel
codes.summary: `expr <- value` where `expr` resolves to a non-channel shape is rejected: a send is only well-typed against a `chan T`, and the accepted-subset contract is that every accepted program emits buildable Go (issue #77 — a void call or other non-channel used as a send target used to pass with 0 diagnostics and then fail `go build`). An UNRESOLVABLE target stays fail-closed under HYB-E3005 (O4.9) instead.
fixits: send to a `chan T` binding (`ch := make(chan T, n)` or a `chan T` parameter)

if the `<-expr` line was meant as a RECEIVE, put the channel expression first: `v := <-ch` — a statement starting with `<-` is a receive, and a `<-` on a new line never continues the previous statement
codes.example: noop() <- 1   // reject: HYB-E3007 — `noop()` is a void call, not a channel

codes.name: chan-direction-mismatch
codes.title: a send to a receive-only channel, or a receive from a send-only channel, is not valid Go
codes.summary: Go's channel direction types (`chan<- T` send-only, `<-chan T` receive-only) constrain what operations the binding allows; the parser and emitter both carry the direction, so sending to a `<-chan T` or receiving from a `chan<- T` (in statements, expressions, select arms, or closure bodies) emits invalid Go that fails `go build` / `go vet` (issue #89).
fixits: declare the parameter/local with the direction the body actually uses (`chan T` for both, `chan<- T` to only send, `<-chan T` to only receive)
if the body needs the opposite operation, widen the declaration to `chan T` (bidirectional) — or split into two channels, one per direction
receives are `v := <-ch` / select recv arms; sends are `ch <- v` / select send arms — check which side of the arrow the misdeclared binding sits on
codes.example: fn worker(ch <-chan int) { ch <- 1 }   // reject: HYB-E3008 — cannot send to a receive-only channel

codes.name: chan-direction-mismatch-op
codes.title: channel direction forbids this operation (close / range)
codes.summary: Channel direction is a type contract the emitter preserves in the Go signature: `close()` requires a bidirectional or send-only channel (a `<-chan T` has no send capability), and `for … in` over a channel requires receive capability (a `chan<- T` cannot be ranged over). Both are invalid Go that `hyb build --emit-go` reproduces faithfully, so accepting them breaks the accepted-should-emit-buildable-Go contract (issue #94).
fixits: declare the channel as `chan T` (bidirectional) where the operation happens
for close: pass a `chan<- T` or `chan T` binding — receive-only channels are closed by their send-side owner
for range: iterate over a `chan T` or `<-chan T` binding — send-only channels are consumed via receives on the other side
codes.example: var rc <-chan int = c; close(rc)   // reject: HYB-E3009 — cannot close a receive-only channel

codes.name: loop-label-out-of-scope
codes.title: `break loop` / `continue loop` has no enclosing loop to target
codes.summary: The `loop` label on `break`/`continue` binds to the nearest enclosing `for`/`loop` statement (SPEC-LANGUAGE LX14). Outside any loop the label has no target: the emitter would lower it to `break hyLoop` / `continue hyLoop` against an undefined Go label, which fails `go vet`/`go build` with `invalid break label hyLoop`. Labels do not cross function or closure boundaries (Go's rule, inherited). Plain `break`/`continue` (no label) inside no loop is separately a parse-level concern; this check covers the labeled form wherever it appears in a checked function body.
fixits: remove the `loop` label — plain `break`/`continue` already targets the innermost enclosing loop
move the statement inside the `for`/`loop` it is meant to exit
if the target is an OUTER loop from inside a nested one, keep `break loop` but ensure the statement is lexically inside that outer loop (the emitter labels the owning loop automatically)
codes.example: fn main() { break loop }   // reject: HYB-E3010 — no enclosing loop

codes.name: channel-element-type-mismatch
codes.title: value does not match the channel's element type
codes.summary: A send `ch <- v` or a typed receive into a binding (`var n T = <-ch`) where the channel's element type and the value/target have CERTAIN, incompatible TypeShape classes (primitive vs string vs named struct vs chan vs map vs slice...) is rejected: the accepted-subset contract is that every accepted program emits buildable Go, and these used to die in `go build` with `cannot use ... as ... value in send` / assignment (issue #146). Channel DIRECTION is checked elsewhere (HYB-E3007 and friends); this rule covers the ELEMENT TYPE. Only certain mismatches are reported — Unknown, opaque/foreign, or unnamed struct shapes stay permissive (a false reject is worse than a missed one). A value already rejected as non-sendable (HYB-E3002) keeps that diagnostic alone — no cascade.
fixits: send a value of the declared element type (`ch <- job{cost: 1}` into `chan job`, or declare `chan int` when sending `7`)
on receive, ascribe the channel's element type (`var n job = <-ch`) or let inference pick it up (`n := <-ch`)

codes.name: chan-direction-coercion
codes.title: channel value cannot convert to the target channel direction
codes.summary: Go's implicit channel conversion is one-way: a bidirectional `chan T` may convert to `chan<- T` or `<-chan T`, but a unidirectional channel (`chan<- T` or `<-chan T`) can never convert to the opposite direction or widen back to `chan T` (issue #623). Passing or assigning a channel with an incompatible direction at a value-flow coercion site (`var`/`const` ascription, assignment, call/task/method/closure argument, return, composite-literal field/element, or channel send/receive of a channel element) emits Go that fails `go vet` / `go build` (`cannot use ... as ... value`). Only certain direction mismatches are rejected — unresolvable shapes fail open.
fixits: declare the source channel as bidirectional (`chan T`) so it can narrow to `chan<- T` or `<-chan T`
change the destination's declared channel direction (`<-chan T` / `chan<- T` / `chan T`) to match the source channel
codes.example:
var sc chan<- int = make(chan int, 1)
var rc <-chan int = sc   // reject: HYB-E3012 — `chan<- int` cannot convert to `<-chan int`

codes.name: go-escape-captured-write
codes.title: closure that writes a captured binding escapes into a foreign Go call
codes.summary: A closure passed as an argument to a package-qualified foreign Go call (`mux.handle(...)`, `time.after_func(...)`) may run on a goroutine the checker never sees, while the closure writes a binding captured from its enclosing Hybrid scope. That is the A5 Go-escape perimeter: the value crosses into Go code that can observe or mutate it concurrently, which no Hybrid spawn/send check covers. The closed-world rule (SPEC-LANGUAGE §8.5 C9, decided W-016) needs no curated Go API database: (1) the closure body writes a captured binding and (2) the closure is passed to a foreign call. The call site must take `managed("...", "interop")`, or the capture must be `const`, or it must be non-may_share.
fixits: wrap the foreign call site in `managed("why", "interop")` so the escape is an auditable decision
make the captured binding `const` so the closure cannot write it
pass a value that carries no shared reference storage (a fresh copy) instead of the captured binding

codes.name: handle-loan-conflict
codes.title: mutating call conflicts with a live borrow loan
codes.summary: A mutating-mode call on a boundary handle conflicts with any live borrow-mode loan on the same handle (O7). Borrow loans live non-lexically, from creation to last use — e.g. across a whole iteration loop.
fixits: collect-then-mutate: gather what you need into locals, let the loan die at its last use, THEN mutate
move the mutating call after the loop
codes.example: for u in doc.array("users")? { doc.set("pruned", true)? }   // reject: HYB-E3101

codes.name: map-slot-loan-invalidated
codes.title: map insert/delete invalidates a live map-slot loan
codes.summary: `svc := &m[k]` is a unique loan on slot k, live from creation to last use (non-lexical). Any insert/delete on the same map inside that window may rehash and move the slot (O8).
fixits: reorder: finish the slot mutation first, then insert
copy-out / modify / store-back (Go-heap reads are copies, O9)
codes.example: svc := &e.services[x]; e.services[y] = v; svc.tag = t   // reject: HYB-E3102

codes.name: borrow-in-field
codes.title: struct fields never hold borrows
codes.summary: Struct fields hold owned values, GC values, ids, or own-handles — never borrows, never borrow-handles (O12). This is why zero annotations is achievable: the #1 annotation-forcing shape is designed out.
fixits: store the index or an id and re-view through the handle at the use site
process the element inside the loop body so the loan dies each iteration
codes.example: struct auditor { cur serde_json.view }   // reject: HYB-E3103 — store a copy or an id

codes.name: loan-escape
codes.title: a loan cannot escape its function
codes.summary: Loans are function-local in Tier 0 (O2): returning `&container[i]` or any borrow from a function is a compile error. A lifetime parameter is deliberately NOT offered — that is the no-visible-lifetimes promise.
fixits: make the mutation a method on the owner so the loan stays in one frame
return the index and let the caller do the access
return a copy (Go-heap reads are copies, O9)
codes.example: return &reg.counters[i]   // reject: HYB-E3104 — loans never escape functions

codes.name: nil-for-non-nilable
codes.title: this type has no nil
codes.summary: nil exists only for `error` and the foreign-Go perimeter. Maps and slices have zero values, not nil (N-rules).
fixits: use the zero value `map[string]int{}` or `[]int{}`
use `option[[]int]` if absence is the meaning
codes.example: var s []int = nil   // reject: HYB-E4001 — use []int{} or option[[]int]

codes.name: enum-no-zero-value
codes.title: this enum has no zero value
codes.summary: An enum's zero value is its first variant only if that variant is payload-free; otherwise `var e E` is a compile error.
fixits: initialize explicitly: `e := some(3)`
reorder variants so the first is the payload-free default
codes.example: var e option[int]   // reject: HYB-E4002 — option[T] has no zero value

codes.name: untyped-nil-declaration
codes.title: an untyped nil cannot declare a binding
codes.summary: `var x = nil` / `x := nil` / `let x = nil` leave the binding with no type at all — Go rejects the emitted declaration outright (`use of untyped nil in variable declaration`), so an accepted program would fail `go build`. nil has exactly two homes (N1): `error` and the foreign-Go perimeter, and both must be visible in a declared type.
fixits: declare the nil home explicitly: `var e error = nil` (error's zero value) or `var h Foreign.handle = nil` at the foreign perimeter (N1/N2)
declare the binding without an initializer — the zero value of the intended type is the value (N3): `var ch chan int`, `var s []int`, `var m map[string]int`
if absence is the meaning, use `option[T]` — its zero value is `none` (N3)
codes.example: var x = nil   // reject: HYB-E4003 — Go: use of untyped nil in variable declaration

codes.name: match-not-exhaustive
codes.title: match is not exhaustive
codes.summary: Every enum match must cover all variants (a `_` arm may be last). The missing variant names are listed in the error.
fixits: add the missing arm(s)
add a final `_` arm if the remaining cases are truly impossible
codes.example: match s { shape::circle => ... }   // reject: HYB-E5001 — missing square/triangle

codes.name: div-by-const-zero
codes.title: division or modulo by constant zero
codes.summary: A `/` or `%` whose divisor is an integer literal `0` is rejected: Go refuses to compile that expression (`invalid operation: division by zero`), so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #149). Only the literal-constant case is in scope — a non-constant zero divisor stays a run-time panic, matching Go.
fixits: replace the constant `0` divisor with a non-zero value
if the divisor is meant to be dynamic, bind it to a variable first — run-time division by zero is a panic, not a compile error
codes.example: y := x / 0   // reject: HYB-E6001 — constant zero divisor; Go cannot build the emitted module

codes.name: const-overflows-fixed-width
codes.title: constant overflows its declared fixed-width type
codes.summary: A local or file-level binding whose declared type is a fixed-width integer and whose initializer is an integer constant outside that type's range is rejected: Go refuses to compile the emitted declaration (`cannot use N as T value (overflows)`), so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #148). The check folds constant EXPRESSIONS too (`100 + 100`, `1 << 10` — Go folds before the range check) and rejects a float constant assigned to an integer type (`var x int = 2.5` → `(truncated)`) (issue #201). Only the constant case is in scope — a variable operand stays a runtime truncation / conversion path (SPEC-LANGUAGE X4).
fixits: use a constant that fits the declared type (e.g. `127` for `int8`, `255` for `uint8`/`byte`)
widen the declared type (e.g. `int16` / `int`) so the constant is representable
if truncation is intentional, convert from a variable (`x := 300; y := int8(x)`) — SPEC X4 defines runtime truncation for non-constant operands
for a float initializer, drop the fractional part or declare a float type
codes.example: var n int8 = 300   // reject: HYB-E6002 — 300 overflows int8; Go cannot build the emitted module

codes.name: const-init-not-constant
codes.title: const initializer is not a constant expression
codes.summary: A `const` binding whose initializer is not a compile-time constant expression is rejected: the emitter keeps the Go `const` keyword for non-composite initializers, so `const c = get_val()` becomes unbuildable Go (`get_val() (value of type T) is not constant`). Composite literals already lower to `var` and are out of scope here (issue #188). Literals, constant arithmetic, references to other `const` bindings, and typed conversions of constant arguments remain accepted (issue #205).
fixits: use a literal or a constant expression (`const c = 42`, `const c = 1 + 2`)
reference another `const` binding instead of a function call or variable
if the value is computed at run time, bind it with `:=` / `let` / `var` instead of `const`
codes.example: const c = get_val()   // reject: HYB-E6003 — call is not a constant expression; Go cannot build the emitted module

codes.name: invalid-array-length
codes.title: array length is not a valid constant
codes.summary: An array length must be a non-negative constant in Go: a negative literal (`[-1]int`), a non-integer constant (`[2.5]int`), or a non-constant name (`[n]int` where `n` is a variable) fails `go build` with `invalid array length`, so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #201). A file-level `const` is a valid length; unknown/computed expressions fail open (they can be legal constant expressions in Go).
fixits: use a non-negative literal or file-level `const` length
declare a slice (`[]T`) when the size is dynamic
codes.example: var a [-1]int  // reject: HYB-E6004 — negative array length; Go cannot build the emitted module

codes.name: negative-shift-count
codes.title: shift by a constant negative count
codes.summary: A `<<` or `>>` (including `<<=` / `>>=`) whose shift count is a constant negative integer is rejected: Go refuses to compile it (`invalid operation: negative shift count`), so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go (issue #201). Only the constant case is in scope — a negative VARIABLE shift count is a run-time panic in Go, matching the compile-error/panic split used for division by zero (E6001).
fixits: shift by a non-negative constant
swap the operands (`1 << n` instead of `n << -1`) when the intent is to shift the other side
codes.example: x := 1 << -1   // reject: HYB-E6005 — negative shift count; Go cannot build the emitted module

codes.name: invalid-const-conversion
codes.title: constant operand invalid for this type conversion
codes.summary: A `Type(const)` conversion whose literal-constant operand Go would refuse is rejected: `int8(300)` on a 64-bit target, `int("abc")`, `string(2.5)`, `float32(1e40)`, `int(10^30)`, `string(true)`, `int8(nil)`, `[]int(3)`, a string constant to a non-byte/rune slice, integer constants of 2^512 or more to `string`, and similar forms fail `go build` on the emitted program (issue #228), so an accepted Hybrid program would emit unbuildable Go. Sub-64 integer overflow (`u8(300)`, SPEC X4) is deliberately accepted — the emitter folds the two's-complement result. Only the literal-constant operand case is in scope; a non-constant operand is a run-time conversion.
fixits: use a constant that fits the target type (e.g. `int8(127)`, `uint8(255)`)
convert between compatible kinds only (number <-> number, string <-> string, `string(65)`, `[]byte("abc")`)
if truncation or a run-time conversion is intended, bind the operand to a variable first (SPEC X4 runtime truncation)
codes.example: x := int8(300)   // reject: HYB-E6006 — constant 300 overflows int8 in Go; the emitted module would not build

codes.name: boundary-pointer-field
codes.title: pointer fields in by-value boundary structs are forbidden
codes.summary: Types crossing the boundary follow the repr(C)-equivalent layout rules (B-rules); pointer fields inside a by-value struct are forbidden — route them as fields per the ABI.
fixits: route the value as an id/handle field instead of a pointer
codes.example: struct crossing { next *node }   // reject: HYB-E7001 for by-value crossing

codes.name: boundary-concrete-types
codes.title: boundary calls need concrete types
codes.summary: A generic (un-instantiated) type cannot cross the boundary; instantiate first.
fixits: instantiate the generic type at the call site first, then cross
codes.example: rust_call(generic_map)   // reject: HYB-E7002 — instantiate first

codes.name: managed-share
codes.title: spawn/send inside a managed block (unchecked share)
codes.summary: The `managed` hatch suppresses the sendability check for this site: the contract is Go's DRF-SC discipline with `-race` as the backstop. Linted and counted by `--report-managed` (O6.3). Warnings can never fail the build.
fixits: prefer the channel redesign (per-task state, merge over a channel)
keep or add a lock if the share is genuinely guarded
accept the hatch knowingly: audit it via --report-managed
codes.example: managed("counter access guarded by a mutex", "mutex") { task tally(counter) }   // warning: HYB-E8001 — unchecked share, counted

codes.name: toolchain-mismatch
codes.title: toolchain does not match the pinned version
codes.summary: `hyb build` enforces the project's version pins (go1.26.9 / Rust 1.99.0 per tools/env.sh) so emitted Go and the compiler behave identically everywhere. The installed toolchain's version differs from the pin. Lints and checks stay available; builds stop.
fixits: install the pinned toolchain version (see tools/env.sh for the exact pins)
source tools/env.sh so PATH picks up the pinned Go at /home/z/tools/go
change the pin deliberately: update tools/env.sh, PLAN.md's environment row, and this registry entry in the same commit
codes.example: hyb build prog.hy -o out/   // reject: HYB-E9001 — go1.21 found, go1.26.9 pinned

codes.name: generate-no-package
codes.title: no Go package beside the .hy file
codes.summary: `hyb generate` emits the transpiled Go INTO the directory's existing package — but .hy files have no package clause BY DESIGN (the emitted file joins the sibling .go files' package). A directory without any `package <name>` clause gives the emitter nothing to join.
fixits: add any .go file with a `package <name>` clause beside the .hy file (or run `hyb vendor-runtime <dir>` for a fresh go.mod project)
an existing go.mod project: point generate at the package directories (go:generate hyb generate ./...)
codes.example: hyb generate ./internal/thing   // reject: HYB-E9002 — ./internal/thing has no .go files; add one with `package thing`
